cat.windows: Windows memory not owned by any process (estimate)
note.secureSystem: Windows security memory (VBS); cannot be turned off.
note.registry: The Windows registry loaded into RAM.
note.memoryCompression: Windows compression store: data of rarely used apps is compressed here to use less RAM. This saves memory, it doesn't waste it.
note.dwm: Draws windows, effects and the interface. Grows with the number of screens and resolution.
note.webview2: Shared web component embedded in Search, Widgets, Teams, Outlook... Not the Edge browser.
note.core: Core Windows process; cannot be turned off.
note.winlogon: Windows sign-in; cannot be turned off.
note.lsass: Security and sign-in; cannot be turned off.
note.wmi: WMI: provides system information to other software.
note.dllhost: Runs COM components (for example, thumbnail generation).
note.vbcscompiler: C# compiler that stays in the background after a build; exits by itself after a few idle minutes.
note.node: Node.js: usually a dev server or developer tool.
note.electronChat: Electron-based chat app: each such app is a separate browser.
note.vietIme: Vietnamese input method (very light, keep it).
note.predatorSense: Acer fan and lighting control software.
note.default.serviceWithServices: Hidden service of Windows or an app.
note.default.service: Runs hidden outside your session (services, system software).
note.default.background: Runs in the background with no window.
kernel.nonpaged.title: Windows kernel: non-paged pool
kernel.nonpaged.note: Memory of the Windows kernel and drivers; always stays in RAM. Unusually large (over 1 GB) usually means a faulty driver.
kernel.paged.title: Windows kernel: paged pool
kernel.paged.note: Windows kernel memory that can be moved to the page file, so not all of it is always in RAM.
kernel.rest.title: Shared, GPU, drivers and other
kernel.rest.note: Memory shared between processes (browsers and Electron apps use a lot), integrated GPU graphics memory, DLLs, page tables, data waiting to be written to disk... Not counted for any single app; closing big apps usually shrinks this too.
adv.browser.off.title: Turn on {0} memory saving (using {1})
adv.browser.off.detail: {0} is holding {1} for tabs and extensions. "{2}" puts tabs you haven't looked at for a while fully to sleep and returns real RAM; when you click the tab again, the page reloads. This is usually the way to reclaim the most RAM without closing anything.
adv.browser.off.detailButton: Click the button below to open the settings page, then turn that option on.
adv.browser.on.title: {0} memory saving is on (using {1})
adv.browser.on.detail: "{0}" is on: tabs you haven't looked at for a while are put to sleep and their RAM is returned. The remaining {1} is tabs you viewed recently, tabs playing audio or video, and extensions. To save more: close tabs, remove unused extensions, or choose a stronger saving level in settings.
adv.browser.builtin.title: {0} is using {1} and already saves memory by itself
adv.browser.builtin.detail: {0} automatically unloads tabs when RAM runs low, so there is nothing to turn on. If it still uses a lot of RAM, close tabs or extensions you don't use.
adv.idle.title: Close {0}: open but unused for {1} min ({2})
adv.idle.detail: {0} is still open, but you haven't used it and it is doing almost nothing. Closing it returns about {1}. The button below closes it normally, like clicking X: the app will ask you to save if needed.
adv.bg.title: Quit {0}: running in the background, using {1}
adv.bg.detail: {0} has no open window but still holds {1}{2}. If you don't need its notifications or sync right now, quit it completely: right-click its icon in the system tray → Quit (safest), or use the button below to force quit.
adv.bg.detailManual: {0} has no open window but still holds {1}. There is no quit button here because this name can cover several separate programs, such as servers, scripts or databases. If you don't need them, stop them from where you started them.
adv.bg.helper: ({0} is the interface part of {1}; closing it alone makes {1} start it again)
adv.startup.title: Stop starting with Windows: {0} ({1})
adv.startup.detail: {0} starts every time you turn on your computer and takes about {1} even before you need it. Turn off auto-start and open it yourself when needed; your computer will also start faster.
adv.compression.title: Windows is compressing {0} of data from rarely used apps
adv.compression.detail: "Memory Compression" is the Windows compression store: data of apps you haven't used for a while is compressed to take less RAM instead of being written to disk (which is much slower). It means Windows is already saving RAM for you; nothing to do.
adv.cache.title: {0} of RAM is working as cache, no need to clean it
adv.cache.detail: Windows keeps recently used file data in RAM so things open faster, and gives it back immediately when an app needs it. This RAM is doing useful work. "RAM cleaner" apps that wipe it only make your computer slower.
adv.upgrade.title: RAM in use {0}%: almost full
adv.upgrade.detail: If this list has suggestions, try them first. If RAM is still often above 85% during normal work, this {0} computer doesn't have enough RAM for what you do, and adding RAM is the only truly effective fix.
